lesson.title: The Event Horizon
lesson.objective: Understand why nothing, not even light, escapes from inside the event horizon.
lesson.approachReason: The event horizon is a threshold defined by a quantity (escape velocity) that changes as an object is compressed, so the clearest path is to let the learner squeeze a star and watch the threshold appear.

blocks.heading: Escape velocity
blocks.body:
Every massive object has an escape velocity: the speed you need to break free of its gravity from a given distance. For Earth at the surface, that's about 11 km/s. The key insight is that escape velocity depends on how tightly the mass is packed — the same mass squeezed into a smaller radius pulls harder at its surface.

This means a star's escape velocity isn't fixed. Compress the star, and the speed needed to leave its surface climbs.
blocks.example: A white dwarf packs the Sun's mass into an Earth-sized ball: its surface escape velocity is thousands of km/s. A neutron star, just 20 km across, is close to half the speed of light.

hints: Think about which object packs its mass closer together.
Escape velocity depends on distance from the mass, not the total amount of mass alone.
blocks.retry: Escape velocity scales as 1/√r: halving the radius multiplies the escape velocity by about 1.4, not 2.

blocks.heading: The line light cannot cross
blocks.body:
In your simulation, at about 3 km the escape velocity reached 300,000 km/s — the speed of light. That's the crucial threshold: light itself is the fastest thing there is, so if even light can't reach escape velocity, nothing can.

The sphere around a mass where the escape velocity equals the speed of light is called the event horizon. Its radius depends only on the mass: for the Sun's mass it's about 3 km, for a ten-solar-mass black hole about 30 km. Inside it, every path leading outward — even a straight beam of light — bends back inward.
blocks.example: This radius was first calculated from Einstein's equations by Karl Schwarzschild in 1916, in the middle of World War I — the Schwarzschild radius is named for him.

hints: Use the threshold you found in the simulation.
The Sun's mass doesn't change — only how tightly it's packed.
blocks.retry: The horizon appears when the escape velocity at the surface hits the speed of light — for the Sun's mass, that happens at about 3 km.

blocks.heading: Earth as a black hole
blocks.prompt: You now have the rule: an event horizon appears when escape velocity reaches the speed of light. Earth's mass is 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg, G = 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Setting escape velocity v = √(2GM/r) equal to c, calculate the event horizon radius Earth would have if it were compressed into a black hole. Give your answer in meters.

traps.feedback: That's the radius in millimeters — Earth's Schwarzschild radius is under a centimeter, about 0.009 m.
You likely kept G and c but forgot to square c: r = 2GM/c², not 2GM/c.

hints: Rearrange √(2GM/r) = c to solve for r.
You should get a number much smaller than 1.
blocks.solution: Solve c = √(2GM/r) for r: r = 2GM/c² = 2 × (6.7×10⁻¹¹)(6.0×10²⁴) / (3.0×10⁸)² = 8.0×10¹⁴ / 9.0×10¹⁶ ≈ 0.0089 m — under a centimeter. Earth's entire mass, collapsed into a marble, would trap light.

blocks.heading: Why nothing gets out
blocks.body:
It's tempting to picture the horizon as a wall that things bump into — but there's no wall. It's a surface in space where the geometry of spacetime itself tips over.

Think of it like a river heading toward a waterfall. Outside the horizon, some currents (directions in space) still flow back upstream, so a powerful enough swimmer — even light — can escape. Inside, every current, even the one pointing 'outward', flows toward the falls faster than anyone can swim. Light isn't slow inside a black hole; it travels at full speed. It's just that space itself funnels inward more steeply than light can climb.
blocks.example: This is why the flashlight experiment from the start of the lesson has only one answer: a beam aimed straight out from inside simply curves back toward the center. There is no outward path left to follow.

hints: Remember the flashlight experiment from the beginning of the lesson.
Light travels at full speed inside — the problem isn't its speed, it's the direction space allows.
blocks.retry: Inside the horizon, all directions in space lead toward the center — there is no outward path for anything, including light, to follow.

blocks.heading: What you now know
points: Escape velocity grows as an object is compressed — same mass, smaller radius, higher speed needed to escape.
The event horizon is the surface where escape velocity equals the speed of light; its radius scales with mass (~3 km per solar mass).
Inside the horizon, nothing can escape — not because things get slow, but because every path through space leads inward.

activities.title: The flashlight experiment
activities.prompt: You hover just inside a black hole's event horizon and shine a flashlight straight outward, away from the center. What happens to the beam of light?
activities.reveal: Inside the horizon, even a beam pointed straight outward curves back inward — light itself cannot reach escape velocity, so nothing can.

options.text: It travels outward forever, since nothing slows light down
options.feedback: Light's speed never changes — but escape velocity here is the speed of light, so traveling outward fast enough isn't possible even for light.

options.text: It curves back around and falls toward the center
options.feedback: Exactly. Inside the horizon there is no outward path — even light aimed straight out bends back inward.

options.text: It slows down, stops, and falls back like a thrown ball
options.feedback: Close on the ending, wrong on the mechanism: light always moves at full speed. It doesn't slow — its path bends back inward.

options.text: It is instantly absorbed by the horizon surface
options.feedback: There is no surface or wall at the horizon — it's a boundary in space, not a physical object.

activities.title: Squeeze a star
activities.prompt: Drag the radius of this object (mass = one Sun) and watch how the escape velocity at its surface changes.
activities.reveal: As the radius shrinks, escape velocity climbs without limit — and at about 3 km it hits the speed of light. That's where an event horizon appears.

bands.title: Event horizon: nothing escapes
bands.detail: Escape velocity here is 300,000 km/s — the speed of light. Even light can't leave. This object is now a black hole.

bands.title: Extreme gravity
bands.detail: Escape velocity is a large fraction of light speed. Matter this compact is a neutron star — gravity strong enough to bend light noticeably.

bands.title: Very dense star
bands.detail: Escape velocity is tens of thousands of km/s — far beyond any rocket, though still well below light speed.

bands.title: Ordinary star
bands.detail: Escape velocity around 600–700 km/s. Enormous by human standards, yet easy compared to what's coming as you compress further.

activities.title: The edge of no return
activities.prompt: You're piloting a ship on a path that will cross a black hole's event horizon. You have fuel for exactly one powerful burn of your engines. What's your best move?
activities.reveal: Outside the horizon, escape is still possible — barely — because the escape velocity hasn't yet reached the speed of light. Once you cross, no engine, however powerful, can change that.

options.text: Burn everything now, while you're still outside the horizon
options.feedback: Correct. Outside the horizon, escape velocity is still finite — a strong enough burn can still get you out. It's your only window.

options.text: Wait until you're just inside the horizon, then burn — a powerful engine can exceed light speed briefly
options.feedback: No engine exceeds light speed, and inside the horizon the escape velocity already exceeds it. Inside, escape is impossible no matter how you burn.

options.text: Cross the horizon and turn around — pointing away from the hole is what matters
options.feedback: Direction doesn't save you. Inside the horizon, even 'straight out' bends back toward the center.

options.text: Turn off the engines — the black hole's pull is weakest at the horizon, so you'll naturally drift away
options.feedback: The opposite is true: at the horizon the escape velocity is the speed of light, the strongest gravity threshold there is.

questions.question: A white dwarf and a neutron star both contain roughly 1.4 times the Sun's mass. The neutron star is about 500 times smaller in radius. Which statement is right?
options: The neutron star has a higher escape velocity, because the same mass is packed into a smaller radius
They have the same escape velocity, because escape velocity depends only on mass
The white dwarf has a higher escape velocity, because it is less dense and gravity spreads out more gently
Neither has an escape velocity, because they are too massive for rockets to leave
questions.correctAnswer: The neutron star has a higher escape velocity, because the same mass is packed into a smaller radius
questions.explanation: Escape velocity rises as radius shrinks at fixed mass — that's exactly what the simulation showed. The tightly packed neutron star's surface escape velocity approaches half the speed of light.

questions.question: Suppose the Sun were magically compressed to a radius of 2 km. What would we observe from a safe distance?
options: An extremely bright, dense star, since the same mass is squeezed harder
A black hole with an event horizon about 3 km across, from which no light escapes
An ordinary-looking but very red star, since gravity stretches light's wavelength
Nothing at all — an object that compact would vanish from the universe entirely
questions.correctAnswer: A black hole with an event horizon about 3 km across, from which no light escapes
questions.explanation: At 2 km, the escape velocity at the surface exceeds the speed of light, so the object sits inside its own event horizon (about 3 km for one solar mass). Light from its surface can never reach us — though the hole's gravity itself is still felt from outside.

questions.question: An astronaut drifts just inside a black hole's event horizon and radios a rescue ship waiting outside, using a powerful transmitter. What reaches the rescuers?
options: A normal message, since radio waves travel at light speed and the astronaut is only just inside
A stretched, fading signal, but the words still get through if the transmitter is strong enough
A redshifted signal that arrives after a long delay — possible with a powerful enough transmitter
Nothing: the signal, like the astronaut, can only follow paths that lead deeper inside
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing: the signal, like the astronaut, can only follow paths that lead deeper inside
questions.explanation: Inside the horizon, the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light, so no signal — no matter how powerful — can reach outward. Every path, including light's, leads inward.

problems: Simulation flaw: the slider has min=1, step=10, so reachable values are 1, 11, 21... — the 3 km horizon band (upTo: 3) is unreachable, yet the lesson tells the learner they watched escape velocity hit light speed at ~3 km in the simulation. The lesson's central claim about the sim never actually happens.

Activity ordering: the flashlight experiment (activity 0) is placed first, before the escape-velocity concept it depends on, and its predict immediately reveals the correct answer — making the later check (ref 2) largely a repeat of what was already given away rather than a genuine test.
Trap feedback error in the Earth problem: 8900 is described as 'the radius in millimeters', but Earth's Schwarzschild radius is ~8.9 mm; 8900 mm would be ~9 m. The feedback's arithmetic is wrong.
The 'edge of no return' scenario (activity 2) is somewhat redundant with the flashlight experiment — both test 'inside = no escape' with the same mechanism, reducing variety.
Minor: check ref 2 tests the flashlight outcome again after the 'Why nothing gets out' explain already states it, so it's a third pass over the same idea.

problems: Simulation band fact error: at the slider's initial 5000 km radius (one solar mass), the surface escape velocity is ~7,300 km/s (v = c·√(r_s/r) = 3×10⁵·√(2.95/5000)), not '600–700 km/s' as the 'Ordinary star' band claims — that figure only applies at the Sun's actual ~700,000 km radius. This directly contradicts what a learner reading the live simulation would see.

Check ref 1's correct answer says 'an event horizon about 3 km across' — 3 km is the Schwarzschild radius, so the diameter is ~6 km. Minor wording slip that could confuse after the lesson carefully established ~3 km as the radius.

The 'Why nothing gets out' river analogy is good, but the promise 'You'll test this directly at the end of the lesson with a flashlight experiment' points to an activity that doesn't exist — check ref 2 is a spaceship-burn multiple-choice, not a flashlight experiment. A dangling forward reference.
